claims.text: The starting W–Cu composites contain residual voids.
The starting W–Cu composites have phase-separated interfaces.
Residual voids and phase-separated interfaces impair thermal conduction under irradiation.
Ultrafast pulsed laser treatment can selectively remelt Cu surrounding W regions.
The proposed laser process locally melts Cu adjacent to W without melting W.
Rapid resolidification fills interfacial voids.
Enhanced interfacial diffusion during laser processing improves contact between Cu and W.
A controlled thermal cycle limits residual thermal-stress accumulation.
Laser remelting produces a resolidified, densified W–Cu interfacial layer.
The densified interfacial layer has significantly reduced porosity.
The densified interfacial layer has stronger bonding between the Cu matrix and W skeleton.
Laser treatment eliminates voids and phase separation.
Laser-treated composites will have lower porosity than untreated SPS- or metal-3D-printed composites.
Laser-treated composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated SPS- or metal-3D-printed composites.
Laser-treated composites will maintain or improve mechanical durability under irradiation relative to untreated SPS- or metal-3D-printed composites.
Conventional SPS fabrication typically leaves residual interfacial voids and heterogeneous phase contacts in W–Cu composites.
Metal 3D printing typically leaves residual interfacial voids and heterogeneous phase contacts in W–Cu composites.
The process is applicable as a post-fabrication treatment for small-scale W–Cu fusion-reactor heat-transfer joints.
Scaling the in situ temperature-control and stress-relief strategy to industrially relevant components may be difficult.
Complex geometries may accumulate residual stress during laser processing.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says mechanical durability will improve, whereas the predicted outcome allows durability merely to be maintained.
